https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/migrants-.text: Jon King Updated Wed, 29 July 2026 at 7:31 am UTC 0 Lithuania's border chief accuses Belarus of allowing migrants to dig tunnels into his country (Image: Getty) Migrants are attempting to enter an EU country via tunnels allegedly built with help from an ally of Russia . The chief of Lithuania 's State Border Guard Service (VSAT), Rustamas Liubajevas, told broadcaster 15min that his staff had found scores of places where underground routes were being dug between his country and Belarus . It comes after VSAT reported discovering a tunnel leading from Belarus into southern Lithuania. He said of the attempts: "Without logistical support from the Belarusian border guards, this would not be possible." Belarus has long weaponised migration, with the country's authoritarian ruler, Alexander Lukashenko, encouraging migrants to use his country to cross into the European Union via the Belarusian border with Latvia, Lithuania and Poland. Mr Liubajevas claimed the Belarusian authorities were either turning a blind eye to or actively helping migrants to dig the tunnels. He added that migrant smuggling attempts through tunnels have increased this year. The chief said similar methods were used on the border between Belarus and Poland. While Belarus and Russia are close allies, Lukashenko has so far kept his country out of Putin's war with Ukraine. Lukashenko allowed Russia to use the country he has ruled since 1994 as a base from which to launch its full-scale invasion in February 2022. But Minsk has been reluctant to get drawn into the war unless Belarus is attacked. The Belarusian leader is reported to have told Russian envoys last weekend that there was "no need" for Belarus to be "drawn into the war". As reported by The Japan Times , he said: "We also don't want to fight Ukrainians. That's why our position is peaceful." Mr Liubajevas's allegation of Belarusian collusion in irregular migration into the EU might suggest Lukashenko wants to continue efforts to add to the migrant crisis affecting the bloc. https://www.politico.eu/article/pedro-sa.text: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s efforts to quell concerns over his government’s handling of the migration crisis in Ceuta fell flat on Tuesday after two of his top ministers publicly clashed over whether vital intelligence warnings were ignored. At the end of July, some 72,000 migrants poured into the Spanish exclave in North Africa, raising major questions about whether Spain’s intelligence services failed to detect the unusually large number of people gathering over the border — something that would have enabled the authorities to deploy more guards. During an emergency hearing in the Spanish parliament on Tuesday, Defense Minister Margarita Robles insisted the National Intelligence Center, which handles both foreign and domestic intelligence and counterintelligence, had issued a warning to the national authorities on July 30, before thousands of migrants started flooding into the exclave. Advertisement Advertisement “Our armed forces, intelligence services, and, of course, the National Intelligence Center carried out the work that was and is required of them, and shared and analyzed this information with the state security forces and the staff of the government delegation,” the minister told lawmakers, defending the work of the agents she oversees. Robles’ statement directly contradicts the Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska’s version of events. For weeks, he has insisted the national government did not reinforce the border in Ceuta because it had no way of anticipating the sudden migrant surge. The minister underscored this point during an extraordinary meeting of the bloc’s interior ministers on Aug. 4, in the aftermath of the influx, where he emphasized Spain’s status as a “strong, reliable partner.” On Tuesday, Grande-Marlaska hit back directly at Robles’ statement during a press conference, insisting that neither Spain’s intelligence services nor any foreign intelligence agents had detected or warned of anything unusual near Ceuta. “There was no report that foreshadowed what ultimately transpired on July 30,” he said, adding that it was a matter of “common sense” that any warning would have been taken seriously and handled accordingly. After lawmakers informed Robles that Grande-Marlaska had denied her statement, the defense minister doubled down and said the country’s intelligence services had warned authorities on July 29, a day earlier than she had originally stated, adding that it was “common knowledge, public knowledge, that people were swimming into Ceuta.” Advertisement Advertisement But she conceded that her agents might have informed national authorities “verbally.” “Intelligence services operate in many ways,” she said. “Often, handwritten reports aren’t necessary.” Detrimental divisions The finger-pointing between two such senior ministers is embarrassing for Sánchez. Nearly a month after the surge, thousands of unauthorized migrants remain in the exclave, and the prime minister is under pressure to prove his government is capable of not only resolving the immediate crisis, but guaranteeing the longer-term security of Spain’s North African exclaves . Sánchez hoped to assuage public fears by convening an emergency meeting of his National Security Council on Tuesday, during which he selected Territorial Policy Minister Ángel Víctor Torres to manage the ongoing response to the crisis. But the attempt to present a united governmental front was upended by Robles and Grande-Marlaska. While infighting within the cabinet is always problematic, the spectacle of two of Sánchez’s longest-serving ministers publicly contradicting each other over what the government knew — and when it knew it — is potentially devastating for a government already under pressure to explain how the crisis was allowed to unfold. Advertisement Advertisement Opposition lawmakers seized on the divisions on Tuesday to accuse Sánchez’s executive of attempting to cover up its botched handling of the crisis. “Marlaska and Robles aren’t even bothering to hide their attempts to accuse one another of lying about the Ceuta crisis,” said Miguel Tellado, secretary-general of the center-right People’s Party. “Spain has been attacked and the prime minister’s response has been to go sunbathing and leave his ministers to fight one another to avoid taking the blame.” Alberto Asarta, lawmaker for the far-right Vox party, went even further and announced he would request Spain’s parliament invoke Article 102 of the constitution, which allows for the prosecution of members of the government. “80,000 people don’t congregate near the border without the intelligence services of Spain and Morocco being aware of it,” Asarta said, adding that the ministers’ failure to protect the exclave “constitutes the crime of treason against the security of Spain.” Advertisement Advertisement

https://japantoday.com/category/features.text: A glass artisan works with molten glass at the Kurokabe glass workshop in Nagahama, Shiga Prefecture. Image: RACHEL TEO travel How Nagahama reinvented itself as a city of glass Sep. 21 06:00 am JST Sep. 22 | 09:22 am JST 3 Comments By Rachel Teo NAGAHAMA, Shiga Nagahama is a historic lakeside city about 40 minutes from Kyoto. Once a thriving merchant center, it is now also known for something with little connection to its feudal past: artisanal glassware. That identity was deliberately created nearly 40 years ago as local leaders searched for a way to revive a struggling city center. From merchant town to decline Meiji Bank, Nagahama Branch, in 1906. Image: Nagahama Hyakunen Located on the shores of the northernmost part of Lake Biwa in Shiga Prefecture, Nagahama was a thriving merchant town in the 1600s. Under the rule of Hideyoshi Toyotomi, a famous feudal lord and one of the Three Great Unifiers of Japan, the city became a prominent trade center thanks to its free market and open guilds. Nagahama was a post town with a booming economy, known for textiles, kimono and a sizable gun manufacturing industry. In 1900, the building became home to Nagahama’s first national bank. Six years later, it housed a branch of Meiji Bank. Incorporating Western-style architecture prevalent during the Meiji era (1868-1912), the building featured black-plastered walls and corbels under the eaves, earning it the nickname kurokabe (“black wall”). Trouble came in the 1960s and 70s with the advent of shopping malls and department stores outside Nagahama city center. The area’s older shotengai (shopping streets) began to steadily decline as visitor numbers dwindled from 150,000 a month to a mere 4,000. By 1988, the shopping streets were deserted, and there was even talk of demolishing the once-grand city landmark of Kurokabe to make way for a new apartment complex. A pedestrian survey in front of the old bank building in April 1988 revealed that only “four people and one dog” passed by in one hour. Building a new identity around glass Kurokabe Glass Shop and Museum. Image: Rachel Teo To save the beloved landmark, Nagahama City Hall officials met with local business leaders, and together they founded a new company, named Kurokabe Corporation, to honor the building’s importance and longstanding presence in the city’s history. “We wanted this new company’s business to combine three core elements: culture and the arts, history, and international appeal,” says Izumi Sato, at Kurokabe Square. Early bids included a kimono exhibition hall, a restaurant, or a hotel – but the company’s president at the time, Sadao Hase, proposed a novel idea: why not turn Kurokabe into an artisanal glassware workshop and venue? Glassware made by Japanese glassware artisans on display for sale. Image: Rachel Teo “Hase’s family business was in textiles and kimono. From his travels in many European countries, he noticed that glass shops and glass studios drew large crowds of people,” says Sato. “He wanted something artistic and cultural to represent [Nagahama], and he thought this might be a great opportunity.” But the other board members struggled to see his vision. Few of them had retail experience, and while glass souvenir items were produced domestically, the quality of glasswork in Japan at the time was not very high. The board members thus decided to visit Europe, trekking from Venice in Italy, to other famous “glass cities” in Germany, Austria, and the Czech Republic. The trip convinced the board that glassmaking could combine the historical, cultural and international elements it wanted for Nagahama. “They thought if they could bring this to Nagahama, they could create a new culture and a new history of glassmaking in the city,” says Sato. Kurokabe Square in Nagahama. Image: Rachel Teo In 1989, Kurokabe Square was born, consisting of a glass shop selling artisanal glassware, a glass studio where people could watch artisans create items from molten glass, and a restaurant. Meanwhile, the city had also recently restored Nagahama Castle, and these two attractions helped to steadily bring visitor numbers back up. “Tourism is extremely important to Nagahama’s local economy,” says Itsuko Umezono, a representative from the Nagahama-Maibara Tourism Association. “The addition of glass gave Nagahama a distinctive identity and helped transform the city [into what it is today].” Trying the glasswork craft Colored glass pieces are laid out for visitors taking part in a glasswork workshop at Kurokabe Square. Image: Rachel Teo At Kurokabe today, visitors can also try their hand at glasswork. The glass studio offers nine different types of workshops, including glassblowing, stained-glass lamp- or photo frame-making, and Edo kiriko (Edo-style glass cutting). Workshop durations range from 30 to 120 minutes, depending on the type of craft. While some creations can be taken home on the same day, creations that involve glassblowing or kiln firing could be mailed to the visitor, or require collection at a later date. “Nagahama attracts many families, senior travelers, and domestic visitors from Kansai, Aichi and Hokuriku,” notes Umezono. “And because of this, we are trying to create workshops that suit a wide variety of visitors,” adds Sato. I tried my hand at glassblowing during one of my visits to the city. I was given a denim apron, thick arm covers and a pair of thick gloves at the studio. I struggled with blowing air into the lump of molten glass and using a variety of metal and wooden tools to shape the lump into something that resembled a bowl. Admittedly, while the expert glassblower did most of the heavy lifting I still found it a very enriching experience. I left with a newfound respect for a simple wineglass, as well as an appreciation of the Nagahama glass artisans’ mastery of the craft. Reviving the city center The large stained-glass murals depicting the city’s Hikiyama Festival at Nagahama station were also made by artisans at Kurokabe. Image: Rachel Teo Nearly four decades after Kurokabe Square opened, the area around Kurokabe has changed with the times, too. The once old and abandoned buildings have been transformed into boutiques, restaurants and stylish cafés. The shotengai, which had once been vacant and desolate, is now a prime spot with businesses vying for a lease. “The city was very careful about what businesses they granted leases for, and they chose businesses around the same three themes,” says Sato, “so [that] they had to be relevant to Nagahama’s history, be artistic in nature or related to the city’s culture, and they had to have some sort of international appeal.” Based on these criteria, many of the shops that fill the shotengai today showcase snippets from Nagahama’s history, including fabrics and textile stores using local materials, and grocers that showcase local produce and meats. There’s even an anime figurine museum, a leather goods store, and a pottery shop, all of which offer their own unique workshops for visitors. These and other boutiques have seen the number of visitors to Nagahama rise as the city continues to change with the times. “Just before COVID hit, Kurokabe Square welcomed its 50 millionth visitor,” says Sato excitedly, “and we’re about to reach 60 million visitors soon!” Editor's note: Currently, the glassblowing studio is temporarily suspended. © Japan Today ©2026 GPlusMedia Inc.
